To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

South Asian pedlars, travelling drapers and toffee men were a significant part of the pre-Windrush South Asian community, that they had a significant impact on the lives of working class communities in the North of England and that they had an important role in the development of the Indian community in the UK.

1) the South Asian pedlars and 'toffee men' were not a homogeneous group; 2) they were not 'immigrants' in the modern sense of the term, having lived in Britain since at least 1900 and in some cases since before 1850; 3) their presence was a direct consequence of the colonial relationship between Britain and India; 4) they were a significant and influential group in their own right, who were able to exert considerable influence

The article also explores the extent to which the South Asian petty traders' networks of trade, sociality and kinship were embedded within the wider British working-class neighbourhoods in which they lived, and the extent to which their presence was accepted, tolerated, and even celebrated by the local communities in which they settled and worked.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the lives and livelihoods of a largely forgotten group of South Asian migrants who were among the first generation of Indians to arrive in Britain.
the lives, livelihoods and legacies of the men who, as the article's title suggests, sold'small things' and'small luxuries' to British working people in the early twentieth century.
the everyday lives of these men and women and the networks that sustained their livelihoods, and in doing so it offers a fresh perspective on the history of South Asian immigration to Britain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
these South Asians were not 'immigrants' in the modern sense of the word, but rather were British subjects who exercised their rights as such.
these men were pioneers of South Asian immigration, trade and enterprise in Britain.
these South Asians were not victims of racism and discrimination but were active participants in the social and economic life of their adopted city.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are trying to understand the lives and livelihoods of South Asian pedlars in Britain, and the networks they created and participated in.

it is a history of the everyday, the ordinary, the unremarkable, but it is a history that has not previously been told, and it is a history which is vital to understanding how and why South Asian migration to Britain took the shape it did.

we have shown how South Asians were not just 'passive' recipients of British colonial rule, but rather active participants in the making of British history, and how their contribution to British society was not just in the fields of science and medicine but also in the fields of business and industry, and in the provision of affordable goods to the British working-class.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the South Asian pedlars and toffee men were not simply passive victims of British colonial and imperial policy, but rather active agents of their own destiny, who used their own networks and social capital to navigate the complex legal, political, social, and economic terrain of early twentieth-century Britain.

the men's success was due to their own ingenuity and entrepreneurialism, rather than the patronage of the British state or the charity of British society, and that the networks they created were the foundation of a more permanent and enduring South Asian presence in Britain.
the 'toffee men' and 'travelling dressers' were not simply passive victims of a British state determined to restrict their movement and livelihoods.
